chapter.title: Throw
chapter.sub: A projector drawn inside a new steel beam — and two documents that can't agree on the lens.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 6 · EPISODE 2 · DRAFT · CASE-032  Design studio · Maya, Anselm, Kit and Odile · Level L4 · Intermediate support  The Playhouse projector is drawn inside a new steel beam — and the throw calculation and the specification can’t agree on the lens.  ⚑ RV-145: structure and mounts are the structural engineer’s. RV-141: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Throw
items.stakes: The Playhouse projector is drawn inside a new steel beam. Two documents disagree on the lens, and the design review is Thursday.
items.reward: A projector position the building allows. One lens schedule. Odile's approval.

objectives.text: Stop it happening on the next set
Look closer: two things about the Playhouse

items.rumor: The beam didn't move into the projector. The projector was drawn into the beam.

items.alt: The Playhouse under renovation: a new steel beam spans the house. Anselm points up at it; Maya holds the projection plan.

bubbles.text: The plan puts the projector nine metres out. The beam is nine metres out.
Then one of them is going to lose.

items.caption: The design review is Thursday.

lines.text: Nine metres from the screen. Nine metres to the beam. Somebody drew a projector inside steel.
And somebody else wrote a spec that puts it somewhere else entirely.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #53 · AVERY'S LENS  One number, one source  Every figure a design depends on should live in one place, and every document that uses it should point there.  The throw calculation said 1.5:1 and the specification said 0.8:1. Two documents, two numbers, one projector — and a beam in the way of both.

items.alt: Back at the studio. Kit, a junior designer, beside a pinned calc sheet that reads D = 1.5 × 6 = 9 m.

bubbles.text: Standard lens, standard answer. It was right when I did it.

items.caption: It was. For a lens nobody specified.

items.prompt: The calc was mine. I used the standard lens — everybody uses the standard lens.

options.label: “Let's re-run it for every lens the family offers and put the cones on Odile's section.”
options.reply: …Every lens. Fine. That's actually faster than arguing.

options.label: “Who wrote the spec line?”
options.reply: Anselm, last month. We never compared.

items.prompt: 10:00. The projector is drawn in the beam. What do you look at first?
items.risk: A projector position nobody can build.
timeout: Kit starts redrawing the projector somewhere random.
Moving it without a reason moves the problem.

hints.text: What does each document actually say?

options.label: Ask the contractor if the beam can be notched
options.result: Odile, cold: “Nobody notches a beam carrying a catwalk.”
options.consequence: Structure isn't a negotiation with the contractor — or with AV.
options.fail: Structural members are the structural engineer's.

options.label: Compare the calc, the spec and the latest sections side by side
options.result: The calc used 1.5:1; the spec calls 0.8:1; section rev C moved the beam to 9 m.
options.consequence: Three documents, three answers — found in ten minutes.

options.label: Shrink the image until it fits somewhere
options.result: The surtitles become unreadable from the back rows.

options.label: Hang it from the beam — it's strong steel
options.consequence: A mount on steel is the structural engineer's decision.

items.title: Two lenses.
items.body: Spec 27 41 00, written by Anselm a month ago: *lens 0.8:1 short-throw, ceiling position.* The calc, written by Kit two weeks later: *standard lens 1.5:1, booth-front.* Two people, two days, no single lens schedule. For a 6 m image, one lens wants 4.8 m and the other 9.
items.label: Test: what's the spec lens's distance — and why did the documents disagree?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Anselm and Maya beside a board. Throw distance is the lens's throw ratio times the image width. Six-metre screen. The standard lens is one-point-five to one… nine metres. The short-throw is point-eight… four-point-eight. And the beam is at nine. Which lens did the calculation use?

bubbles.text: Throw distance is the lens's throw ratio times the image width.
Six-metre screen. The standard lens is one-point-five to one… nine metres. The short-throw is point-eight… four-point-eight.
And the beam is at nine. Which lens did the calculation use?

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Throw ratio   Lens shift   Sightline   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Projector throw distance  D = TR × W   D  lens-to-screen distance, m  TR  throw ratio of the lens (distance ÷ image width)  W  image width, m     ƒ FORMULA · How many times  ratio = A ÷ B   A  the larger (or old) value  B  the smaller (or new) value

items.label: **Learn it now:** throw distance, lenses and sections.

items.title: The magic lantern's arithmetic
items.body: Nineteenth-century lantern shows already worked the same sum: lecturers moved the lantern back to grow the picture, and makers sold objective lenses of different focal lengths so the image fit halls of any size. The throw ratio is that old arithmetic, printed on a data sheet.

items.alt: Section A–A, revision C: the screen at left, the new beam and catwalk 8.7–9.3 m from it, and the projector drawn at 9 m — inside the beam — with its light cone in red.
items.caption: Rev C moved the beam from 11 m to 9 m to carry the new catwalk.

items.title: Rev C · beam relocated
items.body: A small cloud on the section: *beam relocated to carry new lighting catwalk (see S-201 rev C).* The structural sheet was issued the same week as the calc. Nobody on the AV side opened it.

items.title: The beam moved.
items.body: The structural revision came out the same week as Kit's calc: the beam moved from 11 m to 9 m to carry a new lighting catwalk. Kit's 9 m had been clear — for four days.
items.label: Test: what catches a moved beam — and who decides what hangs from it?
**Work it out:** put the projector where the building lets it go.

items.prompt: Wednesday. Three lenses, three distances: 4.8, 9.0 and 10.8 m. What do you propose?
items.risk: A position that needs new structure — or blocks the catwalk.
timeout: Thursday arrives with the projector still in the beam.

hints.text: Which option needs nothing new from anyone else?

options.label: 0.8:1 at 4.8 m on a new ceiling mount I'll detail
1.8:1 at 10.8 m on the existing booth rail; send Odile the cone on her section
options.result: Odile: “Clear of the catwalk and the balcony front. Approved.”
options.consequence: No new steel, serviceable from the booth, numbers attached.

options.label: 1.5:1 at 9 m with the projector just below the beam
options.result: The cone clips the catwalk edge; the bottom of the image is shadowed.
options.consequence: Squeezing past structure isn't a design.

options.label: Let the supplier choose a lens at submittal
options.result: The supplier picks the cheapest lens. It's 1.5:1.
options.consequence: Design decisions don't belong in a submittal.

items.alt: Section A–A with the fix: the projector on the booth rail at 10.8 m with a 1.8:1 lens, its green cone passing clear beneath the beam and catwalk to the full screen.
items.caption: 1.8:1 at 10.8 m. Clear of the steel.

items.prompt: Thursday morning. How do you stop the calc and the spec disagreeing again?
items.risk: The same mismatch on the courthouse.
timeout: The review passes. Nothing else changes.
The next mismatch waits for the next beam.

hints.text: Where should a number live so it can't disagree with itself?

options.label: One lens schedule both documents reference, and every projection cone drawn on the latest section at each issue
options.result: Kit builds the schedule himself and adds the cone check to the issue checklist.
options.consequence: One number, one source — checked on the drawings that show height.

options.label: Anselm checks every calc personally
options.result: Anselm has four projects. He misses one in May.

options.label: Stop writing throw calcs; let suppliers do it
options.result: Suppliers size for their product, not the building.
options.consequence: The design intent leaves the design.

options.label: Nothing — the projector is fixed
options.result: The courthouse set has the same two-document habit.
options.fail: Fix the habit, not only the drawing.

bubbles.text: Your cone is on my section. That's the first projection drawing this year I didn't have to redraw.
It was nearly inside your beam.

items.alt: The Harlow County courthouse, a courtroom under renovation. Priya on the phone, a cost report in her other hand.

bubbles.text: They've value-engineered the second court recorder out. ‘It's a duplicate,’ apparently.

items.caption: Next: *Value-Engineered.*

items.title: An existing position
items.body: The booth rail already has power, a data drop and a service platform — and the architect drew it for exactly this. At 10.8 m, the 1.8:1 lens puts the projector there with no new steel and a technician who can reach it without a lift.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  D = throw ratio × image width. Run it for every lens that could be used, keep one lens schedule that every document references, and draw the cone on the latest section. Anything that hangs is the structural engineer’s; the booth is the architect’s.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Kit’s calc was right for four days. What in your own work is right only until someone else changes something?
